title: The Name
hookLine: don't use God's name carelessly or to justify wrong

cards: Three scenes. Spilled coffee, and someone says, "Oh my God." A handshake over a deal, and someone says, "I swear to God," already planning to break it.
A banner carried into a fight, with God's name stitched across it, as if God had signed up for the side. The same name, three very different uses.
The commandment covers all of them: "Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain." Which of the three does it worry about most?

teach.b: Some readers explain the Hebrew word behind in vain as emptiness, or falsehood: lifting God's name up for nothing, or for a lie.
The verse ends with a warning: "for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain." Christians have read it in more than one direction.
The familiar one: don't use God's name as filler, a curse, an exclamation. The heavier one: don't use God's name to back up something false. A lying oath.
A sermon that blesses a cruelty. A cause that wraps itself in God to win. On that reading, the gravest way to break this commandment isn't a word muttered in traffic.

teach.h: NOT A STAMP ON A WRONG.
teach.b: It's claiming God's backing for a wrong.
Jewish tradition guards the Name with care: in Jewish practice the divine name in scripture is not pronounced aloud, and readers say Adonai, Lord, in its place.
Christians who pray the Lord's Prayer start from the same instinct: "Hallowed be thy name." Hallowed means treated as holy, set apart, handled with care.
And on oaths, as day 245 heard, Jesus says: "let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay."
If your plain word is good, you don't need to drag God in to prop it up. Some Christians, Quakers among them, take that so seriously that they decline to swear oaths at all and affirm instead.
Other Christians take oaths in court and see no conflict with Jesus's words. Both are trying to keep the Name clean.

how: Christians pray "hallowed be thy name" in the Lord's Prayer, and some avoid using God's name as an exclamation; Quakers and some other Christians affirm rather than swear oaths, while other Christians take oaths in court.

games.q: a friend asks you to swear to God you'll keep a promise. following Jesus's words in Matthew 5, what do you do?
o: give a plain yes, and keep it.
games.why: "let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay." a plain word that's kept needs no oath to prop it up.

practice: Run back over the last day or two: how often did the word God come out of your mouth, or your thumbs, without meaning anything at all? Then sit in quiet and let the name rest, unused.
If you pray, you can say it once, slowly, as a prayer, and feel the weight it carries when it isn't spent; if you don't, notice how a word gains weight when it's kept.

wordCard.voice: The Name. God's name, not to be lifted up for nothing, and never used to sign off on something false.

orig.note: Hebrew: in vain, for emptiness. From Exodus 20:7.

carryVoice: Your line: hallowed. A plain yes or a plain no can carry the rest. That's today, done.
